extracted.intended_audience: GAP users, package authors, and programmers writing GAP code
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for writing and understanding GAP programs: lexical structure, identifiers, variables, functions, scopes, evaluation/printing, operator semantics, options, and package namespaces as given in the GAP Reference Manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and processing stages (reading, evaluation, printing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The input (external representation) is transformed by reading into an internal representation (an expression or statement), then transformed by evaluation/execution into a value, and finally printing converts the value back into an external representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every expression has at least one external representation. Reading checks legality according to syntax rules; evaluation replaces expressions by their values recursively (subexpressions first) according to semantic rules; printing converts values to character strings. Knowing the syntactic and semantic rules lets you predict the result of any input. Example: 1 + 2 * 3 is read into a tree, evaluated to 7, then printed as '7'. (See referenced sections for full syntactic and semantic rules.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexical character set
rubrics_metrics.description: Most input consists of sequences of digits, uppercase and lowercase letters, SPACE, TAB, NEWLINE, RETURN and special characters (" . [ ’ / \ ( : ] ) ; ^ * < _ + = { , > } - ~ ! # ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other characters may be used in identifiers by escaping with backslashes, but this feature is not recommended. Inside strings and comments the full character set supported by the computer is allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols and scanning
rubrics_metrics.description: Scanning assembles characters into symbols: keywords, identifiers, strings, integers, and operator and delimiter symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operator and delimiter symbols are explicitly enumerated. During scanning all whitespace is removed (subject to rules about strings/comments). A symbol is a sequence of characters that form a lexical unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whitespace rules
rubrics_metrics.description: SPACE, TAB, NEWLINE, and RETURN are whitespace characters used to separate lexical symbols; two or more adjacent whitespace characters are equivalent to a single whitespace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitespace may occur between any two symbols but not within a symbol. Apart from separating symbols, whitespace is otherwise insignificant (except inside strings where it is significant). Whitespace should be used freely for improved readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments start with # and are whitespace
rubrics_metrics.description: A comment starts with # and continues to the end of the line; the whole comment including the # and the NEWLINE is treated as a single whitespace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inside a string, # is ordinary character and does not start a comment. Examples show that comments may be superfluous but are allowed; comments can be used to make code more readable without affecting parsing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keywords are reserved and case-sensitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Keywords denote special operations or are part of statements and must not be used as identifiers. (The list of keywords is in GAPInfo.Keywords.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Almost all keywords are lowercase and case sensitive: else is a keyword but Else, eLsE, ELSE are identifiers. Keywords must not contain whitespace. Some tokens that look like identifiers (true, false, Assert, IsBound, Unbind, Info, TryNextMethod) are implemented as keywords and cannot be reassigned or have function objects bound to them. The tokens atomic, readonly, readwrite are reserved for future use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifier formation and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An identifier usually consists of letters, digits, underscores _, and at-characters @, must contain at least one non-digit, is terminated by the first character not in this class, and is case sensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The backslash \ can be used to include other characters in identifiers; a backslash followed by a character is equivalent to the character but treated as an ordinary letter. Identifiers starting with a backslash are never keywords. The length of identifiers is not limited, but only the first 1023 characters are significant. The escape sequence \NEWLINE is ignored, allowing splitting long identifiers across lines. Examples of valid identifiers are given (foo, Hello, aLongIdentifier, abc@def, _100).

rubrics_metrics.name: IsValidIdentifier
rubrics_metrics.description: IsValidIdentifier(str) returns true if the string str would form a valid identifier consisting of letters, digits and underscores; otherwise false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IsValidIdentifier does not check whether str contains characters escaped by a backslash. Note that the at-character is used to implement package namespaces for global variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventions about identifier naming (global vs user variables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost every global variable in the GAP library and packages starts with a capital letter; user variables are recommended to start with a lower case letter to avoid name clashes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using capital-starting names for user variables may cause conflicts with predefined globals in newer GAP versions or sessions with loaded packages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressions vs statements
rubrics_metrics.description: An expression is a construct that evaluates to a value; syntactic constructs executed to produce side effects and return no value are called statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressions appear as right hand sides of assignments, actual arguments in function calls, and in statements. Example: '1 + 11' is an expression whose value is integer 12. Statements that execute without return produce no value (procedure calls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primitive expression forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest expressions include variables, function literals, function calls, integer literals, floating point literals, permutation literals, string literals, character literals, list literals, and record literals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These can be combined with operators to form complex expressions. Operators fall into comparisons, arithmetic, and logical classes (see operator table).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator precedence and associativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators are grouped by precedence (from highest to lowest) and associativity: exponentiation ^ (none/ right-to-left for unary +/-, etc.), arithmetic precedence (*,/ mod), binary +/-, comparisons (=, <>, <, <=, >, >=, in), logical operators (not, and, or) with indicated associativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A table lists operators and associativity. Note that < implements a total ordering of objects (useful for sorting) which may not be compatible with inclusion relations (e.g., subgroup relation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable semantics: binding, assignment, and lexical scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A variable is a location pointing to a value; initially an ordinary variable is not bound. Assignment binds a variable to a value; arguments to functions are bound to values upon a call. GAP has lexical scoping: usage of an identifier refers to the variable in the innermost scope with that name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variables differ from variables in compiled languages (no fixed memory blocks; different variables can share the same value). Local scopes range from function keyword to corresponding end. The mapping from identifiers to variables is done when the program is read (lexical scoping). Examples illustrate different variables named the same in different scopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: IsBound for globals and components
rubrics_metrics.description: IsBound(ident) returns true if the variable ident points to a value, false otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For records and lists, IsBound can check whether components or entries are bound. There are also IsBoundGlobal(name) for globals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unbind semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Unbind(ident) deletes the identifier ident; if no other variable points to the same value, that value will be removed by the next garbage collection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unbind can be used to delete components or entries of records/lists. Use with caution: deleting global variables can be confusing for users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global variable facilities: read-only and constant globals
rubrics_metrics.description: Global variables may be marked read-only with MakeReadOnlyGlobal(name) or made constant with MakeConstantGlobal(name). MakeReadWriteGlobal(name) can mark read-only globals read-write again; constants can never be changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warnings are given if name has no value or is already in the requested state. Some GAP optimisations may use constant variables; changing these behaviours may affect printed functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global variable accessor/modifier functions and behaviors
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions like ValueGlobal(name), IsBoundGlobal(name), UnbindGlobal(name), BindGlobal(name,val), BindConstant(name,val), NamesGVars(), NamesSystemGVars(), NamesUserGVars() provide programmatic access and manipulation of global variables by string names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These functions always affect global variables even if local variables with same names exist, and names are passed as strings. BindGlobal makes the variable read-only and prints a warning if name already had a value. UnbindGlobal warns if name was not bound and errors if the global is not writable. Names* functions return sorted lists (immutable where noted). Caution is advised when using these to avoid confusing state changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Package namespaces via @-suffix rule
rubrics_metrics.description: If in package code a global variable that ends with an '@' is accessed, the name of the package is appended before accessing it, implementing a package-local namespace without breaking backwards compatibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Package code is code read with ReadPackage; the package name is taken from PackageInfo.g's PackageName and is case sensitive. Example: a@ in package xYz refers to a@xYz. Code outside the package or interactive input must use a@xYz explicitly. Because @ was not a legal character in earlier releases, this extension is backward-compatible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function literal syntax and local/argument allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Function literals use syntax: function([arg-ident {, arg-ident}]) [local loc-ident {, loc-ident};] statements end. For each formal argument and formal local, a new variable is allocated when the function is called.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A function literal can be assigned and later called. Formal arguments are bound to actual argument values at call time; locals are initially unbound. Recursion is possible because each call gets its own new variables. Examples show iterative and recursive Fibonacci implementations and trade-offs in efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variadic arguments and the special 'arg' identifier
rubrics_metrics.description: Using ... after the last argument denotes variable-length argument lists; the remaining actual arguments are gathered into a list assigned to the final formal argument. A function with a single argument named arg is special-cased as accepting a variable-length list of arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two scenarios: optional arguments and any number of arguments. NumberArgumentsFunction(f) returns minus the number of formal arguments (including final argument) when ... is used. To 'unwrap' a list into arguments use CallFuncList.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorthand function expressions {arg-list} -> expr
rubrics_metrics.description: The shorthand { arg-list } -> expr is equivalent to function ( arg-list ) return expr ; end. Braces may be omitted for single-argument functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is commonly used for short anonymous functions passed to higher-order functions (examples with Sum and Sort).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function call semantics: evaluation order, argument checking, and returns
rubrics_metrics.description: On function call, GAP evaluates the function-var (must be a function), checks that number of actual arguments agrees with formal arguments (except variadic cases), allocates new variables for formals and locals, evaluates actual arguments left-to-right and assigns values, then executes the body. A return with expression yields the function's value; return without expression or completion without return produces no value (procedure call).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the last formal argument is named arg, leftover actual arguments are collected into a list and assigned to arg. Evaluating uninitialized locals signals an error. Examples illustrate calls to library functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function call options mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Options may be supplied after a colon following the actual arguments, with syntax similar to record components; a component name may appear without a value (implying true).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options are evaluated left-to-right but only after all arguments have been evaluated. Options are passed down to subsidiary functions via the global options stack (PushOptions/PopOptions equivalence). Any option may be passed to any function; the system does not guard against misspelled option names. Examples: Size(fpgrp : hard, tcselection := "external") is equivalent to pushing rec(...) then calling Size(fpgrp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparisons semantics and total ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators = and <> test equality and inequality as defined per object type; ordering operators <, <=, >, >= implement a total ordering of objects (definitions per object kinds are in their chapters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objects in different families are never equal. Note that < is a total ordering useful for sorting but may not be compatible with inclusion relations (e.g., subgroup vs ordering).
